title: The principles of general relativity
one_line_summary: Before writing any field equation, the chapter lays out the five heuristic principles behind Einstein's theory (Mach, equivalence, general covariance, minimal coupling, correspondence) and shows how the equivalence principle turns connection coefficients into gravitational forces and the metric into the gravitational potential.
role_in_book: Chapter 9 is the hinge of Part C. Parts A and B supplied special relativity (via the k-calculus) and the full tensor machinery (connections, geodesics, curvature, variational methods), and Chapter 8 recast special relativity as flat Minkowski geometry. This chapter supplies the physical motivation that justifies moving to a curved, non-flat metric: it argues from Newtonian inertial forces and the equality of the three Newtonian masses to the equivalence principle, and from there to the idea that the metric plays the role of gravitational potential and that the field equations should be second-order PDEs in g_ab. It sets up Chapter 10 (non-local lift experiments, geodesic deviation, vacuum field equations), Chapter 12 (minimal coupling of the energy-momentum conservation law), and Chapter 16 (Eotvos experiment, Einstein equivalence principle, Brans-Dicke).

assumed_background.topic: Newton's laws, inertial frames, Galilean transformations between frames in standard configuration
Newtonian gravitational potential, force as minus the gradient of potential, Newton's third law
Centrifugal and Coriolis forces in rotating frames (needed for Exercise 9.2)
Metric connection (Christoffel symbols), metric geodesics, metric flatness
Riemann curvature tensor and its vanishing for a flat metric
Minkowski space-time, Minkowski coordinates, proper time and the free-particle equation
Tensor transformation laws and the idea of a tensor equation
Poisson's equation as a second-order PDE for the Newtonian potential

learning_objectives: Reader can name the five guiding principles of general relativity and say which is regarded as the key one and which are controversial.
Reader can transform Newton's second law into a uniformly accelerated frame and identify the resulting inertial force -ma, noting that it is proportional to the body's mass.
Reader can describe the four phases of Newton's bucket experiment and contrast Newton's absolute-space explanation with Mach's explanation in terms of rotation relative to distant matter.
Reader can state Mach's principle informally and in the three variants M1-M3, and list its main weaknesses (non-quantitative, does not explain why acceleration rather than velocity matters).
Reader can explain why the agreement between the Earth's rotation period relative to local inertial frames and relative to the fixed stars is a Newtonian coincidence that Mach's view explains.
Reader can distinguish inertial, passive gravitational, and active gravitational mass and derive m^I = m^P from universality of free fall and m^P = m^A from Newton's third law.
Reader can state the four versions P1-P4 of the principle of equivalence and explain what 'local' means in them.
Reader can analyse the four lift cases and say which pairs are indistinguishable and which version of the equivalence principle each pair illustrates.
Reader can argue that the Christoffel terms in the geodesic equation play the role of inertial (and hence gravitational) forces, so that the metric acts as a potential and space-time must be curved.
Reader can state the principles of general relativity and of general covariance, explain the 'emptiness' objection, and explain why preferred coordinates can still be useful.
Reader can apply minimal gravitational coupling to generalize a special-relativistic equation (partial derivatives to covariant derivatives, no explicit curvature terms) and recognize its ambiguity.

Reader can draw the correspondence diagram linking general relativity, special relativity, Newtonian gravity and Newtonian mechanics, naming the limits (no gravity; weak field and low speed) on each arrow.

teaching_approach.summary: A discursive, physics-first chapter with almost no new mathematics. It works through Newtonian mechanics to expose 'coincidences' (inertial forces proportional to mass; equal inertial and gravitational mass; inertial frames not rotating relative to the stars) and treats each coincidence as a clue to deeper physics. Principles are stated as labelled, numbered statements (M1-M3, P1-P4), often as statements of impossibility, and the chapter is candid that several of them are philosophically contested. It ends each principle with a pointer to how it is used mathematically later, and the tensor apparatus appears in just two short places: the geodesic equation rewritten in general coordinates (§9.4) and the conservation-law example used to illustrate minimal coupling (§9.6).
narrative_arc: Justify spending a chapter on principles rather than starting from a Lagrangian: principles give insight and a route to repair if the theory fails.
List the five principles and flag which are controversial (Mach, covariance) and which is agreed to be central (equivalence).
Ask whether Newton's laws hold in non-inertial frames; derive the inertial force in a uniformly accelerated frame and note it scales with mass.
Ask how inertial frames are detected: Newton's absolute space and the rotating bucket.

Offer Mach's alternative (inertia from relative motion with respect to distant matter), test it with a rotating universe, the North Pole pendulum coincidence, one-particle and anisotropic universes, the Hughes-Drever null result, and a varying G.
Assess Mach's principle critically and distil three formal variants M1-M3 for later checking against the theory.
Separate the concept of mass into inertial, passive and active; use Galileo's free-fall result and Newton's third law to show all three coincide in Newtonian theory.

Promote the free-fall coincidence to a foundational postulate (P1), add universal coupling (P2), then local indistinguishability of free fall and inertial motion (P3) and of acceleration and gravity (P4).
Illustrate P3 and P4 with Einstein's four lift experiments.

Bridge to geometry: in general coordinates the geodesic equation acquires Christoffel terms that are inertial forces; by equivalence gravity must also live in these terms, so the metric must be non-flat and act as a potential obeying second-order field equations.
Generalize the principle of relativity to all observers and sharpen it into general covariance (tensorial equations), with caveats.
Add minimal coupling as an Occam's razor for porting special-relativistic laws, illustrated with energy-momentum conservation.
Close with the correspondence principle and a diagram of limits.
signature_moves: Treats every Newtonian 'coincidence' as a signal that a deeper principle is at work, and shows how GR turns a Newtonian coincidence into a foundational hypothesis whose failure would sink the theory.

Takes the stance that inertial forces are real because their effects are real (blackouts, shattered flywheels), rather than dismissing them as fictitious, which makes gravity-as-inertial-force natural.
Uses the counterfactual 'hold the bucket fixed and rotate the universe' to separate Newton's and Mach's predictions sharply.
Splits Newtonian mass into three operationally distinct masses and then re-derives their equality, so the reader sees the equality as an empirical input rather than a definition.
States several principles as impossibility statements ('there are no local experiments which ...'), echoing how the principle of relativity is framed.
Numbers competing formulations (M1-M3, P1-P4) explicitly so that they can later be checked against the finished theory.
Reads the Christoffel symbols as force terms and hence the metric components as potentials, borrowing the Newtonian phi / grad phi structure to predict second-order field equations.
Illustrates minimal coupling with a deliberately artificial alternative equation containing the Riemann tensor that also reduces correctly in flat space-time, making the ambiguity concrete.
Frames the correspondence principle as part of scientific modelling: every theory has a domain of validity, drawn as a commutative-looking box diagram of specializations.

sections.title: The role of physical principles
sections.summary: Explains why the authors discuss guiding principles instead of simply postulating a Lagrangian: they illuminate how GR's framework differs from Newtonian and special-relativistic ones and offer a physical basis for repair if the theory fails. Lists the five principles and notes the disputes over their status.
key_moves: Contrasts a Lagrangian-first presentation with a principles-first one and argues for the latter on grounds of insight and robustness.
Cites Einstein's unsuccessful unified-field programme as a cautionary tale of mathematics detached from physical principle.
Records the controversy: covariance called empty by some (Bondi, Fock) but sufficient by others (Anderson); doubt whether GR is Machian; broad agreement that equivalence is the key principle.

sections.title: Mach's principle
sections.summary: Derives the inertial force in a uniformly accelerated frame, then asks what fixes inertial frames. Presents Newton's absolute space and the rotating bucket, Mach's relational alternative, supporting evidence (North Pole pendulum coincidence), consequences (anisotropic inertia, G varying with epoch), the Hughes-Drever null result, criticisms, and three formal versions M1-M3.
concepts: Inertial frames non-rotating relative to the distant stars
Machian variation of the gravitational constant
key_moves: Transforms F = m xddot into frame S' with x = x' + s to get F - ma = m x'ddot, an extra mass-proportional force seen by S'.
Defends inertial forces as physically real and asks for their origin, a question Newtonian theory leaves open.
Walks through the four bucket phases B1-B4 to show concavity tracks the water's rotation, not the bucket's.
Replaces 'rotation relative to absolute space' by 'rotation relative to the fixed stars' and tests the two views with a rotating universe around a fixed bucket.
Uses the equality of the Foucault-type pendulum rotation period and the sidereal rotation period as evidence for Mach.

Argues by reciprocity and a one-particle universe that inertia is set by the global mass distribution, implying anisotropic inertia in an anisotropic universe and a G that depends on the cosmic state.
Weighs the null Hughes-Drever result and CMB isotropy, then lists weaknesses of Mach's idea and states M1-M3.

sections.title: Mass in Newtonian theory
sections.summary: Distinguishes inertial, passive gravitational and active gravitational mass by the roles they play in Newton's second law, in the force on a body in a potential, and in the potential a body produces. Uses equal free-fall acceleration (Pisa, the Moon hammer-and-feather drop) to equate inertial and passive mass, and Newton's third law for two bodies to equate passive and active mass.
concepts: Equality of inertial and passive gravitational mass
Equality of passive and active gravitational mass
key_moves: Defines each mass through the equation it appears in: (9.5), (9.6), (9.7).
Writes m_i^I a_i = -m_i^P grad phi for two dropped bodies; equal accelerations force the ratio m^I/m^P to be universal, set to 1 by choice of units.
Notes the equality is tested to 1 part in 10^12 (forward to §16.3).
Uses the fact that gravity cannot be shielded to consider two mutually attracting bodies; Newton's third law forces m^P/m^A to be universal, set to 1.

sections.title: The principle of equivalence
sections.summary: Defines a gravitational test particle and states four versions of the equivalence principle (P1 universality of free fall, P2 universal coupling, P3 local equivalence of free fall and field-free inertial motion, P4 local equivalence of uniform acceleration and rest in a field). Illustrates P3/P4 with Einstein's four lift experiments and then argues that gravitational forces must reside in the connection of a non-flat metric that acts as a potential.
concepts: Curved space-time from the equivalence principle
Second-order field equations for the metric
key_moves: Contrasts the status of P1 in Newtonian theory (an accommodatable empirical coincidence) and in GR (a hypothesis whose failure refutes the theory).
Extends gravitational coupling to energy via mass-energy equivalence (P2).
Defines 'local' as a region where variations of the gravitational field are unobservable, so a non-rotating freely falling frame recovers special relativity (P3).
Notes the second coincidence (gravity and inertial forces both proportional to mass) and compares mg with ma to motivate P4.
Runs the four lift cases: 1 and 3 indistinguishable (P4); 2 and 4 indistinguishable (P3).
Writes the free-particle equation in Minkowski coordinates and in general coordinates; the Christoffel terms are the inertial forces of a still-flat metric.

Requires gravity also to appear in Gamma; for it to be distinguishable from pure coordinate effects the metric must be non-flat; hence g_ab are potentials and field equations should be second-order PDEs in g_ab.

sections.title: The principle of general covariance
sections.summary: Extends the principle of special relativity to all observers, links observers to coordinate systems, notes that curved space-time has no canonical coordinates, and restates the idea as the requirement that physical equations be tensorial. Acknowledges the objection that any theory can be written tensorially and warns that symmetry-adapted coordinates remain useful.
key_moves: Argues that Earth-bound, non-inertial observers must be able to discover physical laws, so all observers should be equivalent.
Identifies observers with coordinate systems; flatness and integrability of the connection give Minkowski coordinates a canonical status that disappears in curved space-time.
Refines 'any coordinates will do' into 'the theory is invariant under coordinate transformations', i.e. tensorial form.
Notes the retrospective emptiness objection and justifies the Part B tensor digression.

sections.title: The principle of minimal gravitational coupling
sections.summary: Introduces a simplicity rule for carrying special-relativistic equations over to curved space-time: replace partial derivatives by covariant ones and add no explicit curvature terms. Illustrates with energy-momentum conservation and an alternative curvature-containing equation that would equally reduce to the flat-space law.
key_moves: Starts from partial_b T^ab = 0 in Minkowski coordinates.
Offers nabla_b T^ab = 0 as the simplest tensorial generalization.
Exhibits a rival equation with an added Riemann-tensor term that also collapses to the flat law because the curvature vanishes there.
Forbids explicit curvature terms, while admitting the rule was only implicit for Einstein and is vague.

sections.title: The correspondence principle
sections.summary: Places GR within the book's modelling philosophy: a new theory must reproduce older successful theories within their domains. GR must reduce to special relativity without gravity and to Newtonian gravity for weak fields and slow motion, as summarized in a four-box diagram.
concepts: Domain of validity of a physical model
key_moves: Recalls that every model carries a range of validity.
Names the two limits of GR: no gravitation gives special relativity; weak field plus low speed gives Newtonian gravity.
Draws arrows of specialization converging on Newtonian mechanics without gravity.

sections.title: Exercises and further reading
sections.summary: Eleven exercises keyed to §9.2-§9.7 (accelerated-frame mechanics, rotating frames, mass equalities, lift analysis, tidal deformation, geodesics in cylindrical coordinates, light bending by equivalence, minimal coupling, and the c to infinity limit), followed by a short list of other introductory and advanced GR texts.
key_moves: Exercises push the reader to compute pendulum and water-surface tilts in accelerated frames and to derive the general non-inertial equation of motion.
Exercise 9.8 foreshadows gravitational light bending from the equivalence principle alone.
Exercise 9.11 asks for the null cone to be flattened as c grows without bound, linking the correspondence principle to absolute simultaneity.

concepts.name: Heuristic role of physical principles
concepts.definition: The view that a theory's construction is guided by a small set of physical principles which, even when imprecise, constrain its mathematical form and indicate where to look if the theory needs revision.
concepts.how_introduced: Opens the chapter as a defence of the pedagogical choice: one could start from a Lagrangian, but examining Einstein's principles reveals how the framework differs and offers a physically grounded route to repair; Einstein's later fruitless unification attempts serve as the counterexample.

concepts.name: Inertial frame
concepts.definition: A reference frame in which a body free of forces stays at rest or moves uniformly in a straight line, so that Newton's laws hold in their standard form.
concepts.how_introduced: Revisited from Chapter 2 through the question of whether Newton's laws hold in every frame and how the Universe singles out the privileged class in which they do.

concepts.name: Uniformly accelerated reference frame
concepts.definition: A frame S' whose origin accelerates with constant acceleration a relative to an inertial frame S, related (Newtonianly, frames in standard configuration) by x = x' + s(t), y = y', z = z', t = t' with s double-dot = a.
concepts.how_introduced: Set up with Fig. 9.1 using the familiar standard-configuration picture, but with the relative displacement s now accelerating rather than growing linearly.

concepts.name: Inertial force
concepts.definition: An extra force term, proportional to the mass of the body, that appears when Newton's second law is written in terms of accelerations measured in a non-inertial frame; for linear acceleration a it is -ma, and rotating frames give centrifugal, Coriolis and Euler terms.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in two lines by differentiating the accelerated-frame transformation twice and moving ma to the force side. The authors deliberately call these forces real by their effects (astronaut blackouts, bursting flywheels) and use them to pose the question of their physical origin, which Mach tries to answer.
concepts.notes: The key observation carried forward to §9.4 is that every inertial force carries the body's mass as a factor.

concepts.name: Centrifugal and Coriolis forces
concepts.definition: Inertial forces in a frame rotating with angular velocity omega: centrifugal -m omega x (omega x r'), Coriolis -2m omega x r'dot, plus the Euler term -m omegadot x r' when omega varies.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as further examples of inertial forces and left to Exercise 9.2, which derives the full non-inertial equation of motion.
formulas: \mathbf F - [m\mathbf a + 2m\boldsymbol\omega\times\dot{\mathbf r}' + m\boldsymbol\omega\times(\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r') + m\dot{\boldsymbol\omega}\times\mathbf r'] = m\ddot{\mathbf r}'

concepts.name: Absolute space
concepts.definition: Newton's postulated immovable background against which all motion is ultimately referred; inertial observers are those at rest or moving uniformly relative to it, and inertial forces arise from absolute acceleration.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as Newton's answer to 'how do we detect inertial frames?', with a brief quotation of Newton's definition, and immediately operationalized through the bucket experiment.

concepts.name: Newton's bucket experiment
concepts.definition: A suspended bucket of water is spun via a twisted rope; the water surface is flat when only the bucket rotates, becomes concave once the water rotates, stays concave after the bucket stops while the water still turns, and flattens when the water stops. Surface curvature thus tracks the water's rotation, not its rotation relative to the bucket.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as four labelled phases B1-B4 with Fig. 9.2, then extended to linear acceleration (tilted surface, Fig. 9.3), leading to the rule that an observer is inertial exactly when a carried bucket shows a flat surface. It is then reinterpreted in Machian terms.

concepts.name: Mach's principle
concepts.definition: The idea that only relative motion is meaningful and that inertia, inertial forces and the inertial frames themselves are determined by the distribution and motion of all the matter in the universe, dominated by distant matter.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated as the answer to the origin of inertial forces left unanswered by Newton. Built from Berkeley and Mach's relational view, tested against the bucket (rotate the universe instead), supported by the pendulum-at-the-pole coincidence, extended to anisotropic and one-particle universes, critiqued, and finally crystallized into three sharper statements: M1 matter determines the geometry (privileged particle and light paths); M2 no matter, no geometry; M3 a lone body has no inertia.
concepts.notes: The book stresses that GR is at best partly Machian and that Bondi and Samuel catalogue ten versions of the principle; M1-M3 are promised to be checked against the finished theory.

concepts.name: Inertial frames non-rotating relative to the distant stars
concepts.definition: The empirical fact that the frame in which a freely swinging pendulum's plane stays fixed (a local inertial frame) is, to experimental accuracy, non-rotating relative to the distant stars, so the Earth's rotation period measured both ways agrees.
concepts.how_introduced: A pendulum at the North Pole (Fig. 9.4) measures the Earth's rotation relative to absolute space; astronomy measures it relative to the stars; the agreement is an unexplained coincidence for Newton but expected for Mach. Used to launch the methodological maxim that coincidences in a theory signal something fundamental.

concepts.name: Anisotropy of inertia
concepts.definition: A Machian expectation that if matter in the universe were unevenly distributed, a body's inertial response would depend on the direction in which it is accelerated.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached by a reciprocity argument (inertial effects scale with the masses of the inducing bodies) and a one-particle thought experiment (a tiny second mass cannot restore full inertia), illustrated schematically in Fig. 9.5 with different effective masses for accelerations toward and across a concentration of matter.

concepts.name: Hughes-Drever experiment
concepts.definition: Experiments around 1960 by Hughes and by Drever showing that inertial mass is isotropic to at least one part in 10^18, often described as the most precise null experiment ever performed.
concepts.how_introduced: Used as the observational test of anisotropic inertia: its null result means either Mach's principle fails or the universe is highly isotropic, the latter supported by CMB uniformity.

concepts.name: Machian variation of the gravitational constant
aliases: G as a function of epoch
concepts.definition: The inference that, if a body's mass depends on the state of the universe while its potential depends only on the body, then G carries information about the universe and could vary with cosmic epoch or position; a fully Machian theory would let one compute G from cosmic structure.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued from the Newtonian potential phi = -Gm/r by noting that Mach makes m depend on the rest of the universe; used later to motivate Brans-Dicke theory.

concepts.name: Brans-Dicke theory
concepts.definition: An alternative relativistic theory of gravity from the 1960s, intended to be more fully Machian than GR, in which the effective gravitational coupling varies with epoch.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned only in a parenthesis while assessing how far Einstein succeeded in incorporating Mach's principle.
prerequisites: Machian variation of the gravitational constant

concepts.name: Inertial mass
concepts.definition: The mass appearing in Newton's second law, measuring a body's resistance to changes in its motion; a priori it has nothing to do with gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced first of three masses by the equation F = d(m^I v)/dt, with emphasis that nothing links it to gravitation in advance.

concepts.name: Passive gravitational mass
concepts.definition: The mass that measures how strongly a body responds to an externally imposed gravitational field, via F = -m^P grad phi.
concepts.how_introduced: Second of the three masses, defined operationally through (9.6): place the body at a point of known potential phi and the force it feels is proportional to m^P times the potential gradient. The text stresses that this mass, unlike m^I, is tied to gravitation by definition.

concepts.name: Active gravitational mass
concepts.definition: The mass that measures how strong a gravitational field a body produces, via phi = -G m^A / r for a point source.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined as the source strength in the potential of a point mass, completing the three-mass decomposition.

concepts.name: Universality of free fall
concepts.definition: The empirical law, elevated to a principle, that a gravitational test particle's motion in a gravitational field does not depend on its mass or composition; in Newtonian language all bodies at the same place fall with the same acceleration (neglecting air resistance).
concepts.how_introduced: First appears as the observational input of §9.3, credited to Galileo's Pisa drops (Fig. 9.6) and the Moon hammer-and-feather demonstration (Fig. 9.7); then restated in §9.4 as P1 and given a changed status: a mere coincidence in Newtonian theory but a pillar of GR.
concepts.notes: Naming alert: this chapter calls P1 the 'strong' form and P2 the 'weak' form; §16.4 of the same book, like most modern literature, calls universality of free fall the weak equivalence principle.

concepts.name: Equality of inertial and passive gravitational mass
aliases: equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass
concepts.definition: In Newtonian gravity the ratio of inertial to passive gravitational mass is the same for all bodies and can be set to one by choice of units, so m^I = m^P.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by dropping two bodies, writing Newton's second law with the gravitational force for each, and using equal observed accelerations; tested to 1 part in 10^12 as described in Chapter 16.

concepts.name: Equality of passive and active gravitational mass
concepts.definition: In Newtonian gravity the ratio of passive to active gravitational mass is universal and can be set to one, so a body's response to gravity equals its strength as a source.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived from the fact that nothing is shielded from gravity: two isolated bodies attract each other (Fig. 9.8), and Newton's third law applied to the two forces fixes the ratio.

concepts.name: Gravitational test particle
concepts.definition: An idealized body that is acted on by gravity but whose own gravitational influence is negligible, so the field it moves in is fixed in advance.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined at the start of §9.4 so that the free-fall result can be stated cleanly without back-reaction.

concepts.name: Universal coupling of gravity
concepts.definition: The statement that the gravitational field couples to everything: all matter and, by mass-energy equivalence, all energy both responds to and sources gravity, so nothing can be screened from it.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the no-shielding observation of §9.3 and extended to energy using special relativity's mass-energy equivalence; labelled P2.

concepts.name: Freely falling frame
aliases: co-moving frame of a test particle
concepts.definition: A reference frame moving with a gravitational test particle under gravity alone; if in addition it is non-rotating, it is locally an inertial frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the way to 'remove gravity locally' despite universal coupling: fall with the test particles and gravity disappears within a small region. Einstein's 'happiest thought' about a person falling from a roof supplies the image.

concepts.name: Local inertial frame
concepts.definition: A non-rotating freely falling frame restricted to a region small enough that variations of the gravitational field across it cannot be detected; within it test particles move uniformly in straight lines and special relativity holds.
concepts.how_introduced: The book defines 'locally' operationally, as confinement to a region where field variation is unobservably small, anticipating the non-local lift experiments and geodesic deviation of Chapter 10.
concepts.notes: Exercise 9.6 (a falling sphere of dust elongates) probes what goes wrong when the region is not small.

concepts.name: Einstein equivalence principle (local form)
aliases: local indistinguishability of free fall and inertial motion
concepts.definition: Within a small enough region, an observer who is freely falling without rotation cannot tell, by any experiment, that a gravitational field is present: the results match those of an unaccelerated observer far from all matter.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as P3 immediately after defining local inertial frames and phrased as a statement of impossibility; illustrated by lift Cases 2 and 4.
concepts.notes: The label 'Einstein equivalence principle' is the modern name; this chapter only calls it P3. The book's §16.4 gives a separate, more detailed Einstein equivalence principle. Chapter 10 §10.5 revisits freely falling frames.

concepts.name: Equivalence of acceleration and gravitation
aliases: uniform acceleration equivalent to a uniform gravitational field
concepts.definition: Within a small enough region, a reference frame undergoing linear acceleration with respect to a special-relativistic inertial frame cannot be told apart from a frame held stationary in a gravitational field.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by comparing the inertial force ma of (9.3) with the weight mg, both proportional to the body's mass; stated as P4 and illustrated by lift Cases 1 and 3.

concepts.name: Gravity as an inertial effect
concepts.definition: Einstein's reinterpretation of gravity as a force of the same kind as inertial forces, arising because we describe motion from frames that are not freely falling.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the 'other coincidence': of all forces only inertial forces and gravity scale with the mass of the body acted on, suggesting a common origin.

concepts.name: Einstein lift thought experiment
concepts.definition: An observer in a closed windowless room performs local mechanical experiments to determine its state of motion in four situations: accelerating rocket far from masses, coasting rocket, at rest on Earth, and falling freely down an evacuated shaft. A released body falls with g in the first and third, and floats in the second and fourth, so these pairs are indistinguishable.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented after P3 and P4 as their vivid illustration with a matched set of cartoons (Figs. 9.9-9.12), then used as the springboard to curved space-time. Chapter 10 returns to the same four cases with two released bodies to expose tidal (non-local) differences.

concepts.name: Christoffel symbols as inertial forces
concepts.definition: Writing the free-particle equation d^2x^a/dtau^2 = 0 in non-Minkowski coordinates introduces connection terms Gamma^a_bc (dx^b/dtau)(dx^c/dtau); these are exactly the inertial forces of the non-inertial description, even though the metric remains flat.
concepts.how_introduced: Brief bridging argument at the end of §9.4 which identifies 'using a non-inertial frame' with 'using general coordinates' and reads the extra geodesic terms as forces, recalling Chapter 6's metric connection and metric geodesics.

concepts.name: Curved space-time from the equivalence principle
concepts.definition: Because the equivalence principle puts gravitational forces in the same connection terms as inertial ones, and genuine gravity must be distinguishable from a mere change of coordinates in flat space-time, the connection must be the metric connection of a non-flat metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the 'simplest generalization': keep Gamma as a metric connection but drop flatness; justified by the need to separate gravitational from purely coordinate effects.

concepts.name: Metric as gravitational potential
concepts.definition: If the connection coefficients are interpreted as gravitational force terms, then the metric components from which they are built by first derivatives play the role of gravitational potentials, generalizing the Newtonian phi.
concepts.how_introduced: Direct structural analogy: Newtonian force is a first derivative of phi, and Gamma^a_bc is a first derivative of g_ab.
prerequisites: Curved space-time from the equivalence principle

concepts.name: Second-order field equations for the metric
aliases: field equations as second-order PDEs in g_ab
concepts.definition: The expectation that the gravitational field equations of GR, like Poisson's equation for phi, are second-order partial differential equations for the potentials g_ab.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the remaining task at the end of §9.4, pointing forward to Chapter 10.

concepts.name: Principle of general relativity
concepts.definition: All observers, inertial or not, are equivalent in their ability to discover the laws of physics.
concepts.how_introduced: Framed as the logical completion of the special principle of relativity: since we live on a non-inertial Earth, the laws must be discoverable from non-inertial frames too.

concepts.name: Principle of general covariance
concepts.definition: The equations of physics should be expressible in tensorial form, so that they hold in every coordinate system.
concepts.how_introduced: Reached by identifying observers with coordinate systems: curved space-time has no canonical coordinates, so the content of 'all observers are equivalent' becomes invariance of the equations under coordinate transformations. Hedged with two caveats: symmetry-adapted coordinates are still sensible, and any theory can be written tensorially (a point recognized only after GR).
concepts.notes: The book attributes the 'empty' view to Bondi and Fock and the opposite strong view to Anderson.

concepts.name: Canonical coordinate system
concepts.definition: A coordinate system singled out by the geometry itself, such as Minkowski coordinates in flat space-time, which exist globally because the metric is flat and its connection integrable; a generic curved space-time has none.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to explain why special relativity privileges inertial frames and why that privilege lapses in curved space-time, equated with the absence of global inertial observers.

concepts.name: Tensor equation
concepts.definition: An equation between tensors of the same type, which, if true in one coordinate system, is true in all.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked as the mathematical content of general covariance and the reason for the Part B digression into tensors.

concepts.name: Principle of minimal gravitational coupling
concepts.definition: When a special-relativistic law is carried over to curved space-time, add no terms that contain the curvature tensor explicitly. In practice this means writing the law in tensor form (partial derivatives become covariant derivatives, eta_ab becomes g_ab) and stopping there. The book's formal statement is only the no-curvature clause; the derivative-replacement recipe is implied by its example.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the gap left by the earlier principles (they do not tell you how to port a special-relativistic equation), presented as Occam's razor, and illustrated with the conservation law and a rival equation carrying a curvature term that vanishes in flat space-time. Candidly described as implicit in Einstein, vague, and ambiguous.
concepts.notes: The 'comma-goes-to-semicolon' alias is standard elsewhere, not used in this chapter.

concepts.name: Energy-momentum conservation law
concepts.definition: The statement that the energy-momentum tensor has vanishing divergence: partial_b T^ab = 0 in Minkowski coordinates, nabla_b T^ab = 0 in curved space-time.
concepts.how_introduced: Used only as a preview example for minimal coupling; developed properly in Chapter 12.

concepts.name: Riemann curvature tensor
concepts.definition: The tensor built from the connection and its derivatives whose vanishing characterizes a flat metric; any term containing it disappears in special relativity.
concepts.how_introduced: Relied on (from Chapter 6) to show why curvature terms can be added invisibly to a flat-space law, which is what minimal coupling forbids.

concepts.name: Correspondence principle
concepts.definition: A new theory must agree with established earlier theories within their domains of validity: GR must reduce to special relativity when gravity is absent and to Newtonian gravity for weak fields and speeds small compared with light.
concepts.how_introduced: Set in the book's modelling philosophy (every model has a range of validity) and summarized by a box-and-arrow diagram (Fig. 9.13) whose arrows point toward greater specialization.

concepts.name: Newtonian limit
concepts.definition: The regime of weak gravitational fields and speeds much less than c in which GR must reproduce Newtonian gravitation.
concepts.how_introduced: Named here as one arm of the correspondence principle; carried out explicitly in Chapter 10 §10.6.

concepts.name: Tidal effects
concepts.definition: Relative accelerations of nearby freely falling bodies due to spatial variation of the gravitational field, which cannot be transformed away by free fall and set the size limit of a local inertial frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Not developed in the text; implicit in the definition of 'locally' and raised by Exercise 9.6 (a falling sphere of particles changes shape), with full treatment deferred to Chapter 10.

key_equations.name: Transformation to a uniformly accelerated frame
key_equations.latex: x = x' + s, \quad y = y', \quad z = z', \quad t = t'
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian relation between an inertial frame S and a frame S' displaced along x by s(t) with clocks synchronized at coincidence.
key_equations.symbols: s(t): position of the origin of S' in S, with \ddot s = a

key_equations.name: Acceleration transformation
key_equations.latex: \dot x = \dot x' + \dot s, \qquad \ddot x = \ddot x' + \ddot s = \ddot x' + a
key_equations.meaning: Velocities and accelerations measured in S and S' differ by those of the moving origin. (The first relation is garbled in the OCR as \dot x = \dot x + \dot s.)

key_equations.name: Newton's second law viewed from S'
key_equations.latex: F = m\ddot x = m\ddot x' + ma
key_equations.meaning: Substitution of (9.2) into F = m\ddot x.

key_equations.name: Inertial force in a linearly accelerated frame
key_equations.meaning: An accelerated observer who insists on 'force equals mass times my acceleration' must include an extra force -ma, proportional to the body's mass.
key_equations.symbols: F: applied force; m: mass; a: acceleration of S' relative to S

key_equations.name: Newtonian point-mass potential (Machian argument)
key_equations.meaning: Used to argue that G relates a body's mass (Mach: set by the universe) to its potential, so G encodes cosmic information.

key_equations.name: Newton's second law with inertial mass
key_equations.meaning: Defines inertial mass as the quantity whose momentum changes in response to force.
Second law for constant inertial mass.

key_equations.name: Force on a passive gravitational mass
key_equations.meaning: Defines passive gravitational mass as the response coefficient to a gravitational potential gradient.
key_equations.symbols: m^P: passive gravitational mass; phi: gravitational potential

key_equations.name: Potential of an active gravitational mass
key_equations.meaning: Defines active gravitational mass as the source strength of the potential.
key_equations.symbols: m^A: active gravitational mass; r: distance from the source

key_equations.name: Two dropped bodies
key_equations.meaning: Equations of motion for two bodies released at the same place.

key_equations.name: Universal ratio of inertial to passive mass
key_equations.meaning: Equal accelerations force the same ratio for every body; choosing units sets alpha = 1.

key_equations.name: Equality of inertial and passive gravitational mass
key_equations.meaning: Newtonian encoding of universality of free fall; tested to 1 part in 10^12.

key_equations.name: Mutual potentials and forces of two bodies
key_equations.meaning: Each body feels the potential produced by the other.
key_equations.symbols: Q, R: positions of bodies 1 and 2

key_equations.name: Explicit two-body forces
key_equations.latex: \mathrm{grad}_R = \hat{\mathbf r}\,\partial_r = -\mathrm{grad}_Q, \qquad \mathbf F_1 = \frac{G m_1^{P} m_2^{A}}{r^2}\hat{\mathbf r}, \quad \mathbf F_2 = -\frac{G m_2^{P} m_1^{A}}{r^2}\hat{\mathbf r}
key_equations.meaning: With Q at the origin the two gradients are opposite, giving the attractive forces in terms of passive and active masses.
key_equations.symbols: \hat r: unit vector from Q to R

key_equations.name: Equality of passive and active gravitational mass
key_equations.latex: \mathbf F_1 = -\mathbf F_2 \;\Rightarrow\; m_1^{P}/m_1^{A} = m_2^{P}/m_2^{A}\;\Rightarrow\; m^{P} = m^{A}
key_equations.meaning: Newton's third law makes the passive-to-active ratio universal; units set it to one.

key_equations.name: Single Newtonian mass
key_equations.meaning: Why Newtonian theory can speak of just 'the mass' of a body.

key_equations.name: Free test particle in Minkowski coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Straight-line motion of a free particle in an inertial frame of special relativity.
key_equations.symbols: tau: proper time; x^a Minkowski coordinates

key_equations.name: Geodesic equation in general coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Same free motion described in non-inertial coordinates; the connection terms are the inertial forces. Promoted by the equivalence principle to include gravity when g_ab is non-flat.

key_equations.name: Special-relativistic conservation law
key_equations.meaning: Energy-momentum conservation in Minkowski coordinates (developed in Chapter 12).

key_equations.name: Minimally coupled conservation law
key_equations.meaning: Simplest tensorial generalization of (9.10) to curved space-time.

key_equations.name: Non-minimal rival generalization
key_equations.meaning: An alternative equation that also reduces to (9.10) in flat space-time because the Riemann tensor vanishes there; minimal coupling excludes it. As transcribed, index c appears three times and e is free, so the printed index structure appears defective; the point survives with any well-formed curvature term, e.g. \lambda R_{cd}\nabla^a T^{cd}.

figures.label: Fig. 9.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Two frames S and S' at a given moment, with S' accelerating along the shared x-axis.
figures.visual_description: Two right-handed axis triads drawn in perspective: S on the left (x, y, z) and S' on the right (x', y', z'). A horizontal double-headed dimension line labelled s spans the separation of the y and y' axes; a dashed line joins the x-axis to the x'-axis; an arrow at the S' origin points right labelled 'Acceleration a'.
figures.what_it_teaches: Sets up the kinematics for deriving the inertial force: separation s(t) with second derivative a.

redesign.idea: Split-screen cart simulation: left panel shows a ball on a frictionless track in the inertial frame; right panel shows the same motion as recorded by a camera riding an accelerating cart, with a ghost 'inertial force' arrow -ma drawn on the ball.
redesign.interaction: Slider for cart acceleration a and applied force F; toggle 'view from S' / view from S''; mass slider shows that the inertial-force arrow scales with m while the apparent acceleration does not.

figures.label: Fig. 9.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: A bucket of water rotating relative to absolute space.
figures.visual_description: Line drawing of a bucket hanging from a rope, with a circular arrow round the rope above it for the spin and a small twist where the rope meets the handle. The lower part of the bucket is shaded grey for water. The water's top edge is drawn as a straight horizontal line: the figure does not show the concave surface. The curvature appears only in the text (phase B2).
figures.what_it_teaches: The water surface shape reveals rotation; used for phase B2 of Newton's bucket argument.

redesign.idea: 3D bucket simulation with a timeline scrubber through phases B1-B4: bucket and water angular velocities are plotted underneath, and the water surface is a live paraboloid of depth omega^2 R^2/(2g) computed from the water's angular velocity only. Because the printed figure never draws the concavity, the redesign should exaggerate the paraboloid and label its depth.
redesign.interaction: Scrub time or press 'twist and release'; a 'Mach mode' switch holds the bucket fixed and spins a starfield dome around it, with a dial letting the learner choose the Newtonian or Machian prediction for the surface.

figures.label: Fig. 9.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Water in a bucket tilts when the bucket accelerates in a straight line relative to absolute space.
figures.visual_description: Side view of a bucket with shaded water, carried by its handle, with an arrow to the right labelled 'Acceleration a'. The water surface is a straight line tilted so that it is highest at the rear (left) wall and lowest at the leading (right) wall.
figures.what_it_teaches: Linear acceleration also produces a detectable inertial effect, so a bucket of water works as an inertial-frame detector (flat surface if and only if inertial).

redesign.idea: Accelerometer-in-a-cart widget: a bucket and a hanging pendulum in a car share one acceleration slider; the water surface and pendulum both tilt by arctan(a/g), and a second scene of a bucket sliding down a frictionless incline shows the surface aligning with the slope.
redesign.interaction: Drag the acceleration slider or incline angle; readouts show tilt angle vs arctan(a/g); an 'effective gravity' vector g_eff = g - a is drawn and always stands perpendicular to the surface.

figures.label: Fig. 9.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: A pendulum at the North Pole swinging in a frame that does not rotate.
figures.visual_description: A large circle labelled 'Earth' with a small boxed pendulum sitting on top (the North Pole) and a curved arrow drawn across the middle of the globe indicating the Earth's rotation beneath the pendulum.
figures.what_it_teaches: The pendulum plane stays fixed in a non-rotating frame while the Earth turns; its apparent rotation period can be compared with the rotation period relative to the stars.
concepts: Inertial frames non-rotating relative to the distant stars

redesign.idea: Polar Foucault pendulum over a rotating Earth under a star dome: two clocks accumulate the angle the Earth turns relative to the swing plane and relative to the stars, and they tick together.
redesign.interaction: Controls: latitude slider (showing the sin(latitude) slowdown away from the pole), 'rotate stars instead' counterfactual toggle, and a fast-forward; the learner predicts whether the two clocks agree before running.

figures.label: Fig. 9.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: In a universe with more matter in one direction, a body's inertia could depend on the direction it is accelerated.
figures.visual_description: Three axis triads on the left: an inertial frame S at lower left, and two copies of an accelerated primed frame S'. The upper S' has an arrow a pointing up and an inertial-force arrow m_2 a pointing down. The lower-right S' has an arrow a pointing right, towards the matter, and m_1 a pointing left. A callout line connects the two primed frames: the same body, accelerated in two directions. On the right is a large stippled oval labelled 'Preponderance of matter', so m_1 goes with acceleration towards the concentration and m_2 with acceleration across it.
figures.what_it_teaches: Schematic of the Machian prediction of anisotropic inertia (m_1 not equal to m_2) that the Hughes-Drever experiment tests.

redesign.idea: Toy Machian universe: drag clumps of matter around a test body and see a toy inertia ellipse (effective mass vs direction) deform; overlay the Hughes-Drever bound to show how uniform the real universe must be.
redesign.interaction: Drag or add matter clumps; push the body in chosen directions and compare accelerations; a slider sets the fraction of matter in the clump with a readout of the implied anisotropy vs the 10^-18 bound. Clearly labelled as a hypothetical model, not GR.

figures.label: Fig. 9.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Galileo's legendary drops from the Leaning Tower of Pisa (before panel).
figures.visual_description: Cartoon of the tilted, tiered Leaning Tower with a small figure at the top holding out two balls of different appearance (one filled, one open) labelled m_1^I and m_2^I, with the caption 'Before'.
figures.what_it_teaches: Two bodies of different inertial mass released together at the same height.

redesign.idea: Drop lab: release pairs of objects of chosen mass, size and material from a tower with an air-resistance toggle; a hypothetical 'm^I/m^P' dial per object lets the learner break universality and see the objects separate.
redesign.interaction: Choose objects, toggle atmosphere, set the ratio m^I/m^P for each; a timeline shows landing times, and an Eotvos-style readout expresses any separation as a fractional acceleration difference.

figures.label: Fig. 9.6 (after panel)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Galileo's Pisa experiment, after the drop.
figures.visual_description: Same tower cartoon with the figure leaning over the parapet saying 'miracolo!' in a speech bubble; both balls have landed side by side at the base with a 'Splat' mark, captioned 'After'.
figures.what_it_teaches: The two bodies reach the ground together, the empirical basis for equal accelerations.

redesign.idea: Merged into the Fig. 9.6 drop-lab redesign as its outcome state.

figures.label: Fig. 9.7
figures.visual_description: Cartoon of an astronaut in a full spacesuit and helmet, standing face-on with elbows bent: one gloved hand holds a hammer and the other a feather, both at hip height. The 'Before' caption sits below the image in the book rather than inside the drawing.
figures.what_it_teaches: Objects of very different mass and drag are released together where there is no air.

redesign.idea: Side-by-side Earth vs Moon drop of a hammer and feather, with air drag on or off and slow-motion replay; synchronized fall-height graphs make the equal accelerations visible.
redesign.interaction: Toggle location (Earth/Moon/vacuum chamber), play in slow motion, read off g_Moon approx 1.6 m/s^2 from the graph slope.

figures.label: Fig. 9.7 (after panel)
figures.visual_description: The same astronaut with both hands on hips and a speech bubble reading 'How about that!'. The hammer and the feather lie side by side on the ground at the lower left. The 'After' caption is printed below the image.
figures.what_it_teaches: Hammer and feather land together in the airless environment, confirming universality of free fall.

redesign.idea: Outcome state of the Fig. 9.7 Earth-vs-Moon animation.

figures.label: Fig. 9.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: Two isolated bodies attracting each other gravitationally.
figures.visual_description: A horizontal line joining point Q (Body 1) on the left and point R (Body 2) on the right; an arrow labelled F_1 at Q points toward R and an arrow labelled F_2 at R points toward Q.
figures.what_it_teaches: Setup for applying Newton's third law to the mutual gravitational forces, yielding equality of passive and active mass.
concepts: Equality of passive and active gravitational mass

redesign.idea: Two-body 'mass ledger': each body carries three independent sliders (m^I, m^P, m^A); the simulation computes both forces and the centre-of-mass motion, flagging a self-accelerating pair whenever m^P/m^A differs between bodies.
redesign.interaction: Adjust the six masses; watch force arrows grow unequal and the pair run away together when the third law is violated; a 'restore Newton' button snaps ratios to one.

figures.label: Fig. 9.9
figures.caption_paraphrase: Lift experiment Case 1: the lift inside a rocket accelerating far from any masses.
figures.visual_description: A rocket-shaped room (house-like pentagon) with exhaust clouds and nozzles below and an arrow labelled g pointing up from the nose; inside, a stick-figure observer stands beside a released ball with a downward arrow labelled mg.
figures.what_it_teaches: In a uniformly accelerating lift a released body falls to the floor with acceleration g, exactly as on Earth.

redesign.idea: Four-lift equivalence game: the learner sits in a windowless lift in one of the four hidden situations and may drop balls, fire a horizontal ball, or swing a pendulum, then must guess the situation; the reveal shows the outside view. A 'big lift' mode lets two balls far apart reveal tidal convergence, anticipating Chapter 10.
redesign.interaction: Choose experiments inside the lift; toggle 'window' to see the external inertial or Earth frame; slider for lift size to cross from local to non-local.

figures.label: Fig. 9.10
figures.caption_paraphrase: Lift experiment Case 2: the rocket coasting with its engine off.
figures.visual_description: The same pointed-roof room as Case 1 with no exhaust clouds, nozzles or arrows. The observer stands beside a ball drawn in mid-air with no force arrow, and a row of question marks below the base shows the surroundings are unknown.
figures.what_it_teaches: With no acceleration and no gravity, a released body stays at rest relative to the observer.

redesign.idea: One of the four states in the four-lift equivalence game (see Fig. 9.9).

figures.label: Fig. 9.11
figures.caption_paraphrase: Lift experiment Case 3: the lift at rest on the Earth's surface.
figures.visual_description: A rectangular room resting on hatched ground labelled 'Earth'; the observer stands beside a ball with a downward arrow labelled mg.
figures.what_it_teaches: At rest in a gravitational field a released body falls with acceleration g, indistinguishable from Case 1.

redesign.idea: One of the four states in the four-lift equivalence game (see Fig. 9.9).

figures.label: Fig. 9.12
figures.caption_paraphrase: Lift experiment Case 4: the lift falling freely down an evacuated shaft.
figures.visual_description: A room between two hatched shaft walls; the observer and a floating ball are inside; three downward arrows below the room, the middle one labelled g, show the whole lift accelerating downward.
figures.what_it_teaches: In free fall a released body stays at rest relative to the observer, indistinguishable from Case 2: gravity is locally transformed away.

redesign.idea: One of the four states in the four-lift equivalence game (see Fig. 9.9), plus a split view showing the same ball's parabolic path seen from the shaft wall and straight-line rest seen inside.
redesign.interaction: As in the Fig. 9.9 game, with a frame toggle between shaft-wall and lift views.

figures.label: Fig. 9.13
figures.caption_paraphrase: How general relativity reduces to earlier theories.
figures.visual_description: Four rectangular boxes in a 2x2 grid: top-left 'General relativity', top-right 'Newtonian theory of gravitation', bottom-left 'Special relativity', bottom-right 'Newtonian mechanics in the absence of gravitation'. Arrows run from GR right to Newtonian gravitation and down to special relativity, and from each of those to the bottom-right box.
figures.what_it_teaches: Arrows mark specialization: remove gravity (downward) or take weak fields and low speeds (rightward); both routes end at Newtonian mechanics without gravity.

redesign.idea: Theory-space map with two sliders, gravitational field strength (GM/rc^2) and speed (v/c); a marker moves across the four-box square and a sample prediction (e.g. clock rate or orbit precession) morphs continuously as the learner crosses into each simpler theory's domain.
redesign.interaction: Drag the two sliders or pick physical systems (GPS satellite, Mercury, neutron star, lab pendulum) to place the marker; each box highlights when its approximation is within a chosen tolerance.

worked_examples.problem: Find the form of Newton's second law for a particle moving along x as described by an observer in a frame accelerating uniformly along x relative to an inertial frame.
worked_examples.method: Write the Galilean-style transformation with displacement s(t), differentiate twice using t = t', substitute into F = m xddot and move ma to the force side.
worked_examples.key_insight: The non-inertial observer sees a reduced effective force F - ma; the extra term is proportional to the particle's mass, just like gravity.

worked_examples.problem: Show that inertial mass and passive gravitational mass are proportional with the same constant for all bodies.
worked_examples.method: Two bodies released at the same point obey m_i^I a_i = -m_i^P grad phi; equate the observed accelerations and take ratios; repeat for any pair; absorb the universal constant into units.
worked_examples.key_insight: Universality of free fall is precisely the statement that m^I/m^P is universal; the equality is empirical, not logically required.
concepts: Equality of inertial and passive gravitational mass

worked_examples.problem: Show that passive and active gravitational masses are proportional with a universal constant.
worked_examples.method: Write each body's potential with its active mass and the force on the other with its passive mass, evaluate opposite gradients with Q at the origin, and impose Newton's third law F_1 = -F_2.
worked_examples.key_insight: Because gravity cannot be shielded, each body is simultaneously source and receiver; action-reaction then ties the two roles together.
worked_examples.result: m^P = m^A (9.9), hence m = m^I = m^P = m^A
concepts: Equality of passive and active gravitational mass

worked_examples.problem: Determine what an observer sealed in a lift can learn about its state of motion from releasing a body in four situations (accelerating rocket, coasting rocket, on Earth, freely falling).
worked_examples.method: Describe the released body's motion relative to the lift in each case and group cases by identical observations.
worked_examples.key_insight: Cases 1 and 3 match (acceleration mimics gravity, P4); cases 2 and 4 match (free fall erases gravity, P3). Local mechanics cannot reveal the difference.
worked_examples.result: Released body falls with g in Cases 1 and 3; stays at rest in Cases 2 and 4.

worked_examples.problem: Argue from the equivalence principle that gravity requires a non-flat metric that plays the role of potential.
worked_examples.method: Start from d^2x^a/dtau^2 = 0 in Minkowski coordinates; change to general coordinates to obtain Christoffel terms that represent inertial forces; demand by equivalence that gravity also appear there; note that a flat metric would make gravity indistinguishable from a coordinate change; take Gamma to be the metric connection of a non-flat g_ab; interpret g_ab as potentials by analogy with phi and expect second-order field equations.
worked_examples.key_insight: Inertial forces are coordinate artefacts of a flat connection; genuine gravity must be the same kind of term but not removable globally, which is curvature.
worked_examples.result: Space-time is curved; g_ab are the gravitational potentials; field equations should be second-order PDEs in g_ab.
concepts: Curved space-time from the equivalence principle

worked_examples.problem: Generalize the special-relativistic energy-momentum conservation law to curved space-time.
worked_examples.method: Replace the partial derivative by a covariant derivative to get a tensor equation; observe that adding a term containing the Riemann tensor gives another equation with the same flat-space limit; select the one with no explicit curvature.
worked_examples.key_insight: General covariance plus the correspondence limit does not fix a unique generalization; a simplicity principle is needed to exclude curvature couplings.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A carried bucket of water as an inertial-frame detector: flat surface means inertial, curved or tilted surface means rotating or accelerating.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Turns Newton's abstract absolute space into an operational test every observer can perform.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The test works only inside Newtonian mechanics, where gravity counts as an ordinary force. A bucket resting on the Earth's surface shows a flat surface, yet by P3/P4 that frame is not locally inertial. A freely falling bucket, which is locally inertial, has no 'level' surface at all: the water simply floats. After §9.4 the operational test for a local inertial frame is 'released test particles stay put', not 'water is flat'.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Give the learner a virtual bucket they can carry into any simulation (rotating platform, accelerating car, free-falling lift) to test frames.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Christoffel symbols are to the metric what the Newtonian force is to the potential phi.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Because Gamma is built from first derivatives of g_ab, reading Gamma as force makes g_ab the potential, and suggests second-order field equations like Poisson's.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Gamma is not a tensor and can be set to zero at a point; it is not a local physical force field. The invariant gravitational content is curvature (second derivatives), which the analogy does not capture.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Side-by-side panels: phi(x) with -grad phi arrows, and g_00(x) for a weak field with the corresponding Gamma^i_00 arrows, showing they coincide in the Newtonian limit.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Inertial forces are as real as their effects: they black out pilots and burst flywheels.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Motivates asking for a physical origin of inertial forces, and prepares the reader to accept gravity as an inertial force.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Can mislead learners into thinking inertial forces are interactions with a source in the same sense as electromagnetism; in modern GR language they reflect the choice of frame relative to geodesic motion.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Distant stars versus the bucket: a tiny nearby mass matters less than an enormous distant one.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains why the bucket walls barely influence the water's inertia while the far-away but massive fixed stars dominate.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Purely qualitative; Mach supplies no force law, so the relative weights of near and far matter are not computed.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Coincidences in a theory are clues that something deeper is going on.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Recurring methodological refrain tying together the stars-inertial-frame agreement, m^I = m^P, and the mass-proportionality of both inertial and gravitational forces.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: A heuristic, not a proof; some coincidences are just coincidences.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: A 'coincidence board' the tutor fills in as the chapter progresses, each card flipping to reveal how GR explains it.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Frames the rule as a preference for the simplest law consistent with covariance and the flat-space limit.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The book itself warns the rule is vague and ambiguous; for example, ordering of covariant derivatives can matter for fields with second derivatives.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Arrows of specialization in a box diagram of theories.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Shows GR at the apex with two independent simplifications that commute down to Newtonian mechanics.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Limits are not always as clean as arrows suggest (e.g. the c to infinity limit changes the causal structure qualitatively).
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Theory-space map with sliders for field strength and speed (see Fig. 9.13 redesign).

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Inertial (fictitious) forces are mere bookkeeping with no physical significance.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They produce real effects and, crucially, share the defining feature of gravity (proportionality to mass), which is what lets Einstein treat gravity as an inertial effect.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Introductory mechanics teaches that they disappear when one returns to an inertial frame.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Mass is a single property, so equality of inertial and gravitational mass is automatic.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Newtonian theory has three conceptually distinct masses; their equality follows only from experimental facts (universality of free fall) plus the third law.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Textbooks write a single m everywhere and the equality holds to extraordinary precision.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Heavier objects fall faster (the feather falls slower than the hammer because it is lighter).
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The difference on Earth is air resistance; without air, as on the Moon, all bodies share the same acceleration.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Since the equality of inertial and gravitational mass is verified, it must be a theorem of Newtonian mechanics.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In Newtonian theory it is an unexplained coincidence that the theory could survive losing; in GR it is foundational and its failure would refute the theory.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Well-tested facts feel like logical necessities.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The equivalence principle says gravity and acceleration are identical everywhere, so gravity can be globally transformed away.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The equivalence holds only locally, over regions where variations of the field are unobservable; tidal effects remain (Exercise 9.6, Chapter 10).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The lift story is usually told without emphasizing the lift's size.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Nonzero Christoffel symbols mean a gravitational field is present.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Christoffel symbols of a flat metric in non-inertial coordinates are non-zero and represent pure inertial forces; gravity requires the metric itself to be non-flat.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter identifies Gamma with gravitational force terms, which can be over-read.
concepts: Curved space-time from the equivalence principle

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: General covariance means all coordinate systems are equally convenient, so preferred coordinates have no place in GR.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The principle requires tensorial equations, not that every chart is equally useful; symmetry-adapted coordinates are routinely the best choice.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The slogan 'any coordinate system will do'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Writing equations in tensor form is by itself a strong physical constraint that singles out GR.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Almost any theory can be rewritten tensorially; covariance acquires content only alongside other assumptions (no absolute objects, minimal coupling, simplicity).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Einstein named his theory after the principle and it guided him historically.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: General relativity fully realizes Mach's principle.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The book says only that Einstein partly succeeded in building Mach's ideas into GR, and it mentions Brans-Dicke theory as a rival claiming to be more Machian. Supplementary, not stated in this chapter: GR has vacuum solutions with definite geometry (Minkowski, Schwarzschild, gravitational waves), which conflict with M2 and M3, while frame dragging by rotating masses is a partly Machian effect.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Mach was a major inspiration and the principle is often quoted in popular accounts of GR.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Minimal coupling gives a unique, unambiguous curved-space version of every special-relativistic law.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Different tensorial generalizations can share the same flat limit; minimal coupling is a simplicity preference that the book calls vague and ambiguous.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It is often taught as a mechanical 'comma to semicolon' substitution.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The 'strong' equivalence principle is the statement that free fall is independent of mass and composition.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: That is this chapter's labelling of P1, but in the book's own §16.4 and in most modern literature universality of free fall is the weak equivalence principle, while the strong principle extends local equivalence to self-gravitating bodies and all laws of physics.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Reading this chapter in isolation, P1 is explicitly called strong and P2 weak.

thought_experiments.name: Newton's rotating bucket
thought_experiments.setup: A bucket of water on a twisted rope is released and passes through four phases: bucket spinning with flat water, both spinning with concave water, bucket stopped while water still spins and stays concave, both at rest with flat water.
thought_experiments.lesson: Surface curvature is tied to rotation of the water itself, not relative motion with the bucket; Newton took this as evidence for absolute rotation.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Timeline-scrubbable 3D bucket with angular-velocity plots (see Fig. 9.2 redesign).

thought_experiments.name: Fixed bucket in a rotating universe
thought_experiments.setup: Hold the bucket and water still while the entire system of fixed stars rotates around it.
thought_experiments.lesson: Mach predicts a concave surface because only relative rotation matters; Newton predicts a flat one. The counterfactual isolates the difference between the two views.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Star-dome toggle in the bucket simulation asking the learner to commit to a prediction before seeing both theories' outcomes side by side.

thought_experiments.name: Lone particle in an empty universe
thought_experiments.setup: A single particle exists in an otherwise empty universe; then a second particle of tiny mass is added.
thought_experiments.lesson: On Machian grounds the lone particle has no inertia, and the tiny newcomer can restore only a tiny amount, so inertia must be fixed by the total mass and distribution of the universe.

thought_experiments.name: Anisotropic universe
thought_experiments.setup: Imagine most of the universe's matter concentrated in one direction and accelerate a body in different directions.
thought_experiments.lesson: Machian inertia would be direction dependent; the Hughes-Drever null result shows either Mach is wrong or the universe is extremely isotropic.

thought_experiments.name: Einstein's falling observer ('happiest thought')
thought_experiments.setup: A person falls freely from the roof of a house.
thought_experiments.lesson: For the falling observer there is locally no gravitational field: objects released beside them float along.
thought_experiments.app_idea: First-person free-fall scene where dropped keys and a coin hover; switching to the ground camera shows both following identical parabolas.

thought_experiments.name: Einstein's lift experiments
thought_experiments.setup: A windowless room in four states: accelerating rocket in deep space, coasting rocket, at rest on Earth, falling freely in an evacuated shaft; the occupant releases a body.
thought_experiments.lesson: Cases 1 and 3 cannot be told apart locally (P4); Cases 2 and 4 cannot be told apart (P3). This leads to gravity as inertial force and then to curved space-time.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Guess-your-situation lift game with a lift-size slider that reveals tidal effects (see Fig. 9.9 redesign).

thought_experiments.name: Galileo's Pisa drop
thought_experiments.setup: Two bodies of different mass (and composition) are released together from the top of the Leaning Tower.
thought_experiments.lesson: Neglecting air resistance they land together, the empirical basis for universality of free fall and m^I = m^P.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Drop lab with per-object m^I/m^P dials (see Fig. 9.6 redesign).

historical_notes.event: Postulated absolute space as an immovable background and proposed the rotating bucket to detect absolute rotation.
historical_notes.significance: Provided the Newtonian answer to what defines inertial frames, the view Mach and Einstein reacted against.

historical_notes.event: Mach, building on Berkeley's earlier relational ideas, argued that only relative motion is meaningful and that inertia arises from interaction with the rest of the matter in the universe.
historical_notes.significance: Mach's principle strongly shaped Einstein's search for the field equations, although GR ends up only partly Machian. Date note: the book gives 1893, the year of the English edition of Mach's 'The Science of Mechanics'. His critique of absolute space was first published in German earlier (the 1883 'Die Mechanik'), so a learner may meet the earlier date elsewhere.

historical_notes.event: Independent experiments showed mass (inertia) is isotropic to at least one part in 10^18.
historical_notes.significance: Among the most precise null experiments; constrains anisotropic-inertia versions of Mach's principle.

historical_notes.event: Proposed an alternative relativistic gravity theory claimed to be more fully Machian than GR.
historical_notes.significance: Shows Mach's principle still motivating theory-building; revisited in Chapter 16 with PPN tests.

historical_notes.event: Catalogued ten distinct formulations of Mach's principle.
historical_notes.significance: Illustrates how imprecise the principle is and why the book restricts itself to three sample versions.

historical_notes.event: Credited with the Pisa demonstration that bodies of different weight fall together.
historical_notes.significance: Empirical root of universality of free fall and the equivalence principle.

people: Apollo astronaut (unnamed in the book; David Scott, Apollo 15, 1971)
historical_notes.event: An astronaut on the Moon dropped a hammer and a feather together and they landed at the same time.
historical_notes.significance: A vivid airless demonstration of universality of free fall.

historical_notes.event: Realized that a freely falling observer feels no gravitational field, calling it the happiest thought of his life.
historical_notes.significance: Seed of the equivalence principle and hence of GR's geometric view of gravity.

historical_notes.event: Spent much of his later career on unsuccessful mathematical attempts to unify gravitation and electromagnetism.
historical_notes.significance: Used by the authors as a warning about relying on mathematical devices rather than physical principles.

historical_notes.event: Disputed the content of the principle of covariance: Bondi and Fock regard it as empty, Anderson as nearly sufficient to derive GR.
historical_notes.significance: Shows the principles are contested and motivates the book's attempt at precise formulations.

applications_and_observations.topic: Hughes-Drever test of isotropy of inertia
applications_and_observations.details: Null result for direction dependence of inertial mass, interpreted as either refuting Mach's principle or showing the universe is highly isotropic.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Isotropy to at least 1 part in 10^18; around 1960.

applications_and_observations.details: Uniformity of the CMB strongly limits large-scale anisotropy of the universe, supporting the second reading of the Hughes-Drever result.

applications_and_observations.topic: Earth rotation relative to local inertial frames and to the stars
applications_and_observations.details: A pendulum at the North Pole turns relative to the ground once per sidereal rotation, the same period measured relative to the fixed stars, within experimental error.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Two periods agree to experimental accuracy (about one sidereal day).

applications_and_observations.topic: Tests of equality of inertial and passive gravitational mass
applications_and_observations.details: Eotvos-type torsion balance experiments (detailed in §16.3) verify m^I = m^P.

applications_and_observations.topic: Hammer and feather on the Moon
applications_and_observations.details: Airless demonstration that bodies of very different mass and shape fall together.

applications_and_observations.topic: Physiological and engineering effects of inertial forces
applications_and_observations.details: Large accelerations cause astronaut blackouts and centrifugal stresses can shatter flywheels, cited to argue inertial forces are physically real.
